questions.questionText: You need to securely connect an on-premises network to a Google Cloud VPC over the public internet. The connection must support dynamic routing and offer a 99.99% availability SLA. Which service should you choose?

explanation.general explanation: HA (High Availability) VPN securely connects your on-premises network to your VPC network through an IPsec VPN connection over the public internet. It uses BGP for dynamic routing and provides an industry-leading 99.99% service availability SLA when configured correctly.

why other options are wrong.Classic VPN: Classic VPN only provides a 99.9% SLA, uses single tunnels, and is being deprecated in favor of HA VPN.
why other options are wrong.Dedicated Interconnect: Dedicated Interconnect provides a private, dedicated connection, but it does not traverse the public internet.
why other options are wrong.Partner Interconnect: Partner Interconnect uses a service provider to create a private connection, bypassing the public internet.

questions.questionText: Your company wants to connect its on-premises data center directly to Google Cloud using a private network connection. You require a minimum bandwidth of 10 Gbps and want to completely avoid routing traffic over the public internet. Your data center is located in a Google-supported colocation facility. What should you use?

explanation.general explanation: Dedicated Interconnect provides a direct, physical connection between your on-premises network and Google's network. It is designed for enterprise-grade connections that require high bandwidth (10 Gbps or 100 Gbps circuits) and requires you to be in a supported colocation facility.

why other options are wrong.Partner Interconnect: Partner Interconnect is used when your data center is NOT in a supported colocation facility or when you need lower bandwidth capacities (like 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps).
why other options are wrong.HA VPN: HA VPN routes encrypted traffic over the public internet, which violates the requirement to avoid the public internet.
why other options are wrong.Direct Peering: Direct Peering connects your network to Google's edge to access Google Workspace and public APIs, not your internal VPC resources.

questions.questionText: Your organization needs a private connection to Google Cloud with a bandwidth of 1 Gbps to securely access VPC subnets. Your data center is NOT located in a Google-supported colocation facility. Which hybrid connectivity option is best suited for this scenario?

explanation.general explanation: Partner Interconnect provides private connectivity to Google Cloud through a supported service provider. It is the ideal solution when your data center is outside of Google's colocation facilities and you want a private connection that doesn't use the public internet, especially for sub-10 Gbps bandwidths.

why other options are wrong.Dedicated Interconnect: Dedicated Interconnect requires you to have physical routing equipment inside a Google-supported colocation facility.
why other options are wrong.HA VPN: HA VPN encrypts traffic over the public internet rather than providing a dedicated private circuit.
why other options are wrong.Carrier Peering: Carrier Peering is a legacy service for reaching public Google APIs, not internal VPC subnets.

questions.questionText: You are configuring an IPsec VPN between your on-premises router and Google Cloud. You want Google Cloud to automatically advertise new VPC subnets to your on-premises network without requiring manual updates to the VPN configuration. Which Google Cloud service must you configure to enable this?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Router enables dynamic routing for your VPC network using the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). When connected to a Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect, it automatically exchanges network topology information with your on-premises router, seamlessly advertising new subnets as they are created.

why other options are wrong.Cloud DNS: Cloud DNS resolves domain names; it does not handle IP network route advertisements.
why other options are wrong.Cloud NAT: Cloud NAT allows private VMs to access the public internet; it does not perform hybrid dynamic routing.
why other options are wrong.VPC Peering: VPC Peering connects two different Google Cloud VPCs together, not on-premises networks to GCP.

questions.questionText: You are setting up an HA VPN to connect your Google Cloud environment to an on-premises data center. Which two components are strictly required in Google Cloud to establish this dynamic, highly available connection?
options: A Global External Application Load Balancer

explanation.general explanation: To set up an HA VPN, you fundamentally need two components on the Google Cloud side: an HA VPN Gateway (which provides the IPsec endpoints) and a Cloud Router (which uses BGP to dynamically manage the routes across the tunnels).

why other options are wrong.A Cloud NAT Gateway: Cloud NAT is used for outbound internet access for private VMs, not for establishing IPsec VPNs.
why other options are wrong.A Dedicated Interconnect connection: Dedicated Interconnect is an alternative physical connection method; it is not required to create a VPN.
why other options are wrong.A Global External Application Load Balan: Load balancers distribute user traffic to backends; they are not used to terminate IPsec VPN connections.

questions.questionText: Your on-premises applications need to resolve internal domain names configured in a Google Cloud DNS private managed zone. How should you configure Cloud DNS to allow on-premises systems to query these Google Cloud domain names over your VPN?
options: Enable DNSSEC on the private zone
Configure a public managed zone instead

explanation.general explanation: A Cloud DNS inbound server policy provides an internal IP address within your VPC that acts as a DNS resolver. Your on-premises DNS servers can forward queries for Google Cloud domains to this IP address over your VPN or Interconnect, allowing on-prem systems to resolve GCP private domains.

why other options are wrong.Create an outbound server policy: An outbound policy is used for the reverse scenario: allowing Google Cloud VMs to resolve on-premises DNS names.
why other options are wrong.Enable DNSSEC on the private zone: DNSSEC provides cryptographic validation of DNS records but does not provide cross-network resolution paths.
why other options are wrong.Configure a public managed zone instead: Using a public zone would expose internal infrastructure names to the public internet, compromising security.

questions.questionText: Your Google Cloud Compute Engine instances need to resolve hostnames for legacy servers located in your on-premises data center. The on-premises network is connected to Google Cloud via Cloud Interconnect. How should you configure Cloud DNS?
options: Create a private zone with an outbound server policy and forwarding rules pointing to on-premises DNS servers
Create a public zone with an inbound server policy
Use Cloud NAT to translate DNS requests to the on-premises IP addresses
Configure the /etc/hosts file on every Compute Engine instance manually
correctAnswers: Create a private zone with an outbound server policy and forwarding rules pointing to on-premises DNS servers

explanation.general explanation: To allow GCP resources to resolve on-premises hostnames, you must create an outbound server policy in Cloud DNS. You also configure a DNS forwarding zone that explicitly tells Cloud DNS to forward requests for the on-premises domain to the on-premises DNS server IP addresses.

why other options are wrong.Create a public zone with an inbound ser: Inbound policies allow on-prem to query GCP, not the other way around. Public zones expose data to the internet.
why other options are wrong.Use Cloud NAT to translate DNS requests: Cloud NAT is for outbound public internet access, not internal cross-network DNS resolution.
why other options are wrong.Configure the /etc/hosts file on every C: This is completely unscalable and prone to error, violating cloud architecture best practices.

questions.questionText: Your on-premises servers need to upload large backup files to a Google Cloud Storage bucket. You have a Dedicated Interconnect configured. For security and cost reasons, this traffic must traverse the Interconnect and not the public internet. What feature should you enable and configure?
options: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts
Cloud NAT on the VPC network
VPC Network Peering to the Cloud Storage bucket
correctAnswers: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts

explanation.general explanation: Private Google Access for on-premises hosts allows on-premises systems to connect to Google APIs and services (like Cloud Storage) over an existing Cloud Interconnect or Cloud VPN connection, keeping the traffic entirely off the public internet.

why other options are wrong.Cloud NAT on the VPC network: Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access for VMs inside GCP. It does not route on-premises traffic to Google APIs.
why other options are wrong.Serverless VPC Access connector: This connector bridges serverless environments (like Cloud Run) into a VPC, which is unrelated to on-premises traffic.
why other options are wrong.VPC Network Peering to the Cloud Storage: Cloud Storage is an API service; you cannot configure VPC Peering directly to a Cloud Storage bucket.

questions.questionText: You are planning to provision a Dedicated Interconnect to link your enterprise data center to Google Cloud. Which two prerequisites must be met by your organization before the physical connection can be fully established?
options: You must have routing equipment located in a Google-supported colocation facility
You must order a cross-connect from the colocation provider to Google's equipment
You must configure an active HA VPN connection as a permanent backup
You must use an external service provider to manage the BGP sessions
You must allocate a public /24 IP block for the Interconnect VLAN attachments
correctAnswers: You must have routing equipment located in a Google-supported colocation facility
You must order a cross-connect from the colocation provider to Google's equipment

explanation.general explanation: Dedicated Interconnect requires your organization to physically reach Google's network. Therefore, you must have your own routing equipment in a Google-supported colocation facility and you must work with the facility provider to provision a physical cross-connect cable from your router to Google's edge router.

why other options are wrong.You must configure an active HA VPN conn: While highly recommended for temporary backup during provisioning, it is not a strict prerequisite to establish the Interconnect itself.
why other options are wrong.You must use an external service provide: In Dedicated Interconnect, your organization manages the BGP sessions directly. Service providers are used in Partner Interconnect.
why other options are wrong.You must allocate a public /24 IP block: VLAN attachments use link-local private IP addresses (169.254.0.0/16), not public /24 blocks.

questions.questionText: Due to strict defense compliance regulations, your hybrid connection must be both physically private (not traversing the public internet) AND cryptographically encrypted at the network layer. Which architecture meets these exact requirements?
options: Classic VPN over the public internet

explanation.general explanation: HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect combines the benefits of both services. It uses Cloud Interconnect to ensure the traffic travels over a dedicated, private physical circuit, and it runs IPsec VPN tunnels on top of that circuit to provide strict cryptographic encryption, fulfilling rigorous compliance standards.

why other options are wrong.Classic VPN over the public internet: This traverses the public internet, violating the physical privacy requirement.
why other options are wrong.Dedicated Interconnect configured with B: While private, standard Dedicated Interconnect traffic is not cryptographically encrypted by default (unless MACsec is explicitly supported/used). HA VPN over Interconnect guarantees IPsec encryption.
why other options are wrong.Direct Peering: Direct Peering connects over the internet exchange and is not encrypted natively by IPsec.

questions.questionText: You need to increase the bandwidth of your existing HA VPN connection. A single VPN tunnel provides a maximum of 3 Gbps, but you need 6 Gbps of throughput. How can you reliably achieve this increased capacity using Cloud VPN?
options: Add more VPN tunnels and configure Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing
Upgrade the VPN Gateway tier to Premium in the console
Change the VPN routing protocol from BGP to static routing
Enable jumbo frames on the VPN gateway configuration
correctAnswers: Add more VPN tunnels and configure Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing

explanation.general explanation: To scale VPN bandwidth beyond the 3 Gbps limit of a single tunnel, you must provision multiple VPN tunnels and use Cloud Router to distribute traffic across them using Equal-Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing. This allows the bandwidth of multiple tunnels to aggregate.

why other options are wrong.Upgrade the VPN Gateway tier to Premium: There is no 'Premium' tier for VPN gateways that magically increases single-tunnel throughput.
why other options are wrong.Change the VPN routing protocol from BGP: Static routing does not increase bandwidth and is actually incompatible with the dynamic nature of ECMP for HA VPN.
why other options are wrong.Enable jumbo frames on the VPN gateway c: Jumbo frames increase MTU size but do not overcome the hard 3 Gbps limit per IPsec tunnel.

questions.questionText: Your company is migrating to Google Cloud and has configured a Dedicated Interconnect. The VPC contains subnets in the `us-central1` and `europe-west1` regions. The Interconnect is physically connected in `us-central1`. Currently, the on-premises network can reach instances in `us-central1` but cannot reach instances in `europe-west1`. What should you change in your VPC configuration?
options: Change the VPC network's dynamic routing mode from Regional to Global
Create a secondary Dedicated Interconnect in the europe-west1 region
Enable Cloud NAT in the europe-west1 region
Configure VPC Peering between the two regions
correctAnswers: Change the VPC network's dynamic routing mode from Regional to Global

explanation.general explanation: When a VPC's dynamic routing mode is set to Regional (the default), Cloud Router only advertises subnets located in the same region as the router. Changing the dynamic routing mode to Global tells the Cloud Router to advertise all subnets across all regions to the on-premises network.

why other options are wrong.Create a secondary Dedicated Interconnec: While a second interconnect improves redundancy, simply changing routing to Global allows immediate cross-region access without expensive hardware purchases.
why other options are wrong.Enable Cloud NAT in the europe-west1 reg: Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access, which is irrelevant to private internal hybrid routing.
why other options are wrong.Configure VPC Peering between the two re: VPC Peering connects different VPCs. Subnets in different regions within the *same* VPC already have connectivity; the issue is BGP advertisement to on-prem.

questions.questionText: What is a strict routing protocol requirement for your on-premises edge router when configuring an HA VPN connection to Google Cloud?
options: It must support Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)
It must support Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
It must support Routing Information Protocol (RIP)
It must support static policy-based routing only
correctAnswers: It must support Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)

explanation.general explanation: HA VPN strictly requires the use of dynamic routing using the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP). Your on-premises VPN device must support BGP to peer with the Google Cloud Router and establish the highly available paths.

why other options are wrong.It must support Open Shortest Path First: Cloud Router does not support OSPF for dynamic route exchange.
why other options are wrong.It must support Routing Information Prot: Cloud Router does not support RIP.
why other options are wrong.It must support static policy-based rout: HA VPN does not support static or policy-based routing; these were only supported by the deprecated Classic VPN.

questions.questionText: You are reviewing an architecture diagram that shows a Google Cloud environment connected to an on-premises network. The connection explicitly uses MACsec for line-rate, hardware-level encryption. Which Google Cloud hybrid connectivity service supports this specific feature natively?

explanation.general explanation: Cloud Interconnect (specifically Dedicated Interconnect and Cross-Cloud Interconnect) supports MACsec for Cloud Interconnect. MACsec provides point-to-point, line-rate hardware encryption on the physical circuit, offering high security without the overhead of IPsec.

why other options are wrong.HA VPN: HA VPN uses IPsec for encryption, not MACsec. IPsec operates at Layer 3, whereas MACsec operates at Layer 2.
why other options are wrong.Cloud CDN: Cloud CDN is a content delivery network, unrelated to hybrid point-to-point connections.
why other options are wrong.Cloud Router: Cloud Router handles BGP routing logic, but the physical MACsec encryption occurs on the Interconnect hardware.

questions.questionText: Referencing the EHR Healthcare case study: They need to connect their existing on-premises legacy systems to Google Cloud to securely transmit high volumes of sensitive patient data. They require a highly reliable, private connection with SLA guarantees to meet healthcare compliance, avoiding public internet routing. Which option aligns best with their business requirements?

explanation.general explanation: EHR Healthcare requires high volume (bandwidth), high reliability (SLA guarantees), and strict privacy (avoiding the public internet for sensitive data). Dedicated Interconnect meets all these criteria by providing a private, SLA-backed, high-bandwidth physical connection to Google Cloud.

why other options are wrong.Classic VPN: Classic VPN traverses the public internet, which violates the requirement for a private, off-internet connection.
why other options are wrong.Direct Peering: Direct Peering is for accessing Google's edge (public APIs/Workspace) and does not provide an SLA.
why other options are wrong.Cloud NAT: Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access for cloud VMs, which does not provide hybrid connectivity to on-premises networks.

questions.questionText: When configuring Private Google Access for on-premises hosts over a Cloud Interconnect, which two actions are strictly required to ensure traffic correctly reaches Google APIs?
options: Configure on-premises DNS to resolve `*.googleapis.com` to the restricted or private virtual IP (VIP) ranges
Advertise the restricted or private Google API IP ranges to your on-premises network via Cloud Router
Assign external public IP addresses to all on-premises hosts
Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway in the VPC
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) on all API endpoints
correctAnswers: Configure on-premises DNS to resolve `*.googleapis.com` to the restricted or private virtual IP (VIP) ranges
Advertise the restricted or private Google API IP ranges to your on-premises network via Cloud Router

explanation.general explanation: To enable Private Google Access for on-premises hosts, you must route traffic destined for Google APIs through the Interconnect. This requires configuring your on-prem DNS to resolve API calls to the specific Google VIPs (restricted or private), and configuring Cloud Router to advertise those VIP IP ranges back to the on-premises network so the routers know where to send the packets.

why other options are wrong.Assign external public IP addresses to a: The whole point of this feature is to allow hosts with *internal* IP addresses to securely reach Google APIs without needing public IPs.
why other options are wrong.Deploy a Cloud NAT gateway in the VPC: Cloud NAT is for allowing GCP VMs to reach the external internet. It is not used for routing on-premises API traffic.
why other options are wrong.Enable Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) on all: IAP is for zero-trust access to web apps and SSH/RDP, not a routing requirement for accessing Google APIs.

questions.questionText: You need to achieve a 99.99% availability SLA for your Dedicated Interconnect architecture. What is the minimum topology required by Google Cloud to qualify for this strict SLA?
options: Two interconnect connections located in two different metropolitan areas
Two interconnect connections located in the same metropolitan area
A single interconnect connection with a secondary HA VPN backup
A single interconnect connection with dual cross-connects
correctAnswers: Two interconnect connections located in two different metropolitan areas

explanation.general explanation: To achieve the highest 99.99% SLA for Dedicated Interconnect, Google Cloud mandates a highly redundant topology. You must provision at least two interconnect connections, and they must be placed in two different metropolitan areas (metros) to protect against a catastrophic regional failure.

why other options are wrong.Two interconnect connections located in: This topology only qualifies for a 99.9% SLA because a metro-wide failure could still disconnect you.
why other options are wrong.A single interconnect connection with a: While a good practice for resilience, this specific mix does not formally qualify for the 99.99% Dedicated Interconnect SLA.
why other options are wrong.A single interconnect connection with du: A single connection provides no SLA. If that one Google edge router goes down for maintenance, you lose connectivity.

questions.questionText: You need to achieve a 99.9% availability SLA for your Dedicated Interconnect architecture. What is the minimum topology required by Google Cloud to qualify for this SLA?
options: Two interconnect connections located in the same metropolitan area
A single interconnect connection with no backups
Two interconnect connections located in different regions
correctAnswers: Two interconnect connections located in the same metropolitan area

explanation.general explanation: For a 99.9% SLA, Google Cloud requires at least two Dedicated Interconnect connections. These can be located within the same metropolitan area (connected to different edge availability domains/routers) to ensure redundancy against single hardware failures.

why other options are wrong.A single interconnect connection with no: A single connection has no SLA guarantee because routine Google maintenance on that edge router will cause downtime.
why other options are wrong.Two interconnect connections located in: This actually qualifies for the higher 99.99% SLA, not the minimum required for 99.9%.
why other options are wrong.Four interconnect connections spread glo: This is overkill for a 99.9% SLA and is generally used for global, ultra-resilient 99.99% setups.

questions.questionText: You are configuring a VLAN attachment for a Dedicated Interconnect. You need to assign IP addresses to the BGP peering interfaces on the Cloud Router and your on-premises router. What type of IP address range must be used for this point-to-point connection?
options: A public IP address block assigned by IANA
A subnet from your primary VPC internal IP range

explanation.general explanation: VLAN attachments for Cloud Interconnect require a point-to-point IP link between the Cloud Router and your on-premises router to establish BGP. Google Cloud requires you to allocate an IP address range from the link-local 169.254.0.0/16 space (specifically a /29 block) for this peering session.

why other options are wrong.A public IP address block assigned by IA: Interconnect is a private connection; public IPs are not used for internal BGP peering.
why other options are wrong.A subnet from your primary VPC internal: Using VPC subnets for BGP peering interfaces is not supported for VLAN attachments and would cause routing conflicts.
why other options are wrong.A loopback address block (127.0.0.0/8): Loopback addresses are strictly for local machine testing and cannot be used to route traffic across a physical network link.

questions.questionText: You are troubleshooting a newly created HA VPN connection. The IPsec tunnels are showing as 'Established' in the console, but your on-premises network cannot ping or reach the Google Cloud VPC subnets. What are two likely causes of this issue?
options: The BGP session on the Cloud Router is not established
The VPC firewall rules are blocking inbound traffic from the on-premises IP range
IKEv2 is not supported by the on-premises router
The Cloud VPN gateway does not have a public IP address
correctAnswers: The BGP session on the Cloud Router is not established
The VPC firewall rules are blocking inbound traffic from the on-premises IP range

explanation.general explanation: If the IPsec tunnels are 'Established', the cryptographic negotiation phase was successful. The inability to pass traffic is usually a Layer 3 or security issue. Either the BGP session hasn't formed (so routes aren't exchanged), or the VPC firewall rules are implicitly denying the inbound traffic from the on-prem network.

why other options are wrong.The pre-shared key (PSK) is mismatched: A mismatched PSK would cause the IPsec tunnel negotiation to fail completely. The tunnel would not show as 'Established'.
why other options are wrong.IKEv2 is not supported by the on-premise: If IKEv2 wasn't supported, the VPN tunnel phase 1 negotiation would fail, and it would not be 'Established'.
why other options are wrong.The Cloud VPN gateway does not have a pu: HA VPN gateways are automatically provisioned with public IPs. If it lacked one, the tunnel could not form.

questions.questionText: Your company wants to connect Google Cloud directly to Microsoft Azure using Google's dedicated infrastructure, bypassing the public internet to ensure high bandwidth and low latency for a multi-cloud application. Which service provides this specific multi-cloud connectivity?

explanation.general explanation: Cross-Cloud Interconnect is a specialized Google Cloud service designed specifically to connect your Google Cloud network directly to another cloud provider's network (like AWS, Azure, or OCI) using Google's dedicated hardware, ensuring low latency and high bandwidth without the public internet.

why other options are wrong.Partner Interconnect: Partner Interconnect uses a third-party service provider to connect your on-premises data center to GCP, not directly to another cloud provider's backbone.
why other options are wrong.HA VPN: HA VPN encrypts traffic over the public internet, which violates the requirement to bypass the public internet.
why other options are wrong.VPC Peering: VPC Peering only connects VPC networks *within* Google Cloud, not across different cloud providers.

questions.questionText: You have an existing Partner Interconnect connecting your on-premises data center to Google Cloud. The service provider experiences an outage, bringing down the connection. Who is primarily responsible for providing support and managing the SLA for the physical connection between your data center and the service provider's network?

explanation.general explanation: In a Partner Interconnect arrangement, the Service Provider manages the connection from your data center to their network, and then from their network into Google. If there is a physical failure on the provider's side, the Service Provider is responsible for troubleshooting and upholding the SLA for that segment.

why other options are wrong.Google Cloud Support: Google Cloud Support is only responsible for the infrastructure within Google Cloud (the VLAN attachment and Cloud Router), not the partner's physical circuit.
why other options are wrong.Your internal network team: While they manage your internal network, they do not manage or provide the SLA for the external service provider's circuit.
why other options are wrong.The colocation facility provider: The colocation provider houses equipment but does not manage the end-to-end network service SLA.

questions.questionText: Your Google Cloud VPC network has a primary IP range of `10.10.0.0/16`. You are planning to set up an HA VPN to your on-premises data center, which currently also uses the IP range `10.10.0.0/16`. What is the most robust architectural solution to establish this connection without causing routing conflicts?
options: Re-IP either the VPC network or the on-premises network so the CIDR blocks do not overlap
Use Cloud NAT to translate the traffic going to the on-premises network
Configure VPC Peering instead of HA VPN
Enable dynamic routing on the Cloud Router to automatically resolve conflicts
correctAnswers: Re-IP either the VPC network or the on-premises network so the CIDR blocks do not overlap

explanation.general explanation: Overlapping IP spaces cause severe routing conflicts in hybrid networks because routers cannot distinguish between the local and remote destinations. The best practice and most robust architectural solution is to re-IP (change the subnet ranges) one of the environments to ensure the CIDR blocks are completely distinct.

why other options are wrong.Use Cloud NAT to translate the traffic g: While complex NAT workarounds exist, Cloud NAT natively provides outbound internet access, not bidirectional hybrid connectivity resolution. Re-IP is the standard best practice.
why other options are wrong.Configure VPC Peering instead of HA VPN: VPC Peering does not connect on-premises environments, and it strictly prohibits overlapping IP ranges anyway.
why other options are wrong.Enable dynamic routing on the Cloud Rout: Cloud Router uses BGP to share routes, but it cannot magically resolve fundamental IP address overlap conflicts. It will simply fail to route traffic correctly.

questions.questionText: You are configuring Cloud Router for your HA VPN connection. You want your on-premises network to route all of its outbound internet traffic through your Google Cloud VPC environment so you can perform centralized security inspection. What should you configure the Cloud Router to advertise to the on-premises network?
options: The Google API restricted IP range

explanation.general explanation: To force all outbound traffic from an on-premises network to traverse the VPN into Google Cloud, you must configure the Cloud Router to advertise a custom default route (`0.0.0.0/0`). This tells the on-premises routers that the path to 'everywhere' is through Google Cloud.

why other options are wrong.The VPC's internal subnet ranges: Advertising the internal subnets only allows on-prem to reach internal GCP resources, not the public internet.
why other options are wrong.The Google API restricted IP range: This only allows on-prem to reach Google APIs (like GCS), not the general public internet.
why other options are wrong.The Cloud DNS forwarding zone: DNS forwarding resolves domain names; it does not dictate IP packet routing paths.

questions.questionText: Mountkirk Games is looking to securely connect their external data analytics partners to their Google Cloud environment. The partners do not have a presence in a Google colocation facility but require a dedicated private connection rather than an internet-based VPN. Which two components will be involved in this hybrid networking setup?
options: A service provider network (the partner's carrier)
correctAnswers: A service provider network (the partner's carrier)

explanation.general explanation: Because the partner requires a private connection but is not located in a Google-supported colocation facility, the correct solution is Partner Interconnect. This setup relies on a third-party service provider network (the carrier) to bridge the physical gap between the partner's location and Google Cloud.

why other options are wrong.Dedicated Interconnect: This requires the partner to have equipment directly inside a Google-supported colocation facility, which the scenario explicitly excludes.
why other options are wrong.Cross-Cloud Interconnect: This connects Google Cloud directly to AWS/Azure/OCI, not to a general external business partner's data center.
why other options are wrong.HA VPN: The scenario specifically states they require a dedicated private connection rather than an internet-based VPN.

questions.questionText: You want to establish an HA VPN connection. When you create the HA VPN gateway resource in the Google Cloud Console, what does Google Cloud automatically provision to facilitate the two required IPsec tunnels?

explanation.general explanation: When you create an HA VPN gateway, Google Cloud automatically provisions two external IPv4 addresses (one for each interface). These public IPs act as the secure termination endpoints for the two IPsec tunnels coming from your on-premises network.

why other options are wrong.A Cloud Router: While required for BGP, the Cloud Router is a separate resource you must create and attach; it is not provisioned automatically as part of the Gateway object itself.
why other options are wrong.A /29 link-local IP range: Link-local ranges are used for BGP peering within Cloud Router or VLAN attachments, not directly provisioned by the VPN Gateway creation.
why other options are wrong.A Cloud NAT instance: Cloud NAT is an entirely different service for outbound internet access and is unrelated to VPN creation.

questions.questionText: You are migrating applications from on-premises to Google Cloud. During the migration, both environments need to communicate. You have ordered a Dedicated Interconnect, but the physical circuit provisioning will take several weeks. What is the standard practice to establish hybrid connectivity immediately while waiting for the Interconnect?
options: Provision an HA VPN over the public internet as a temporary measure
Use Direct Peering for temporary private access
Set up a Serverless VPC Access connector to the on-premises data center
Use Cloud CDN to cache data between the environments
correctAnswers: Provision an HA VPN over the public internet as a temporary measure

explanation.general explanation: Because HA VPN traverses the public internet, it can be provisioned in minutes. It is standard practice to use HA VPN to establish immediate, secure connectivity while waiting for the lengthy physical installation process of a Dedicated Interconnect.

why other options are wrong.Use Direct Peering for temporary private: Direct Peering also requires physical provisioning and is not used for VPC access.
why other options are wrong.Set up a Serverless VPC Access connector: This connects serverless apps to a VPC; it does not connect an on-prem data center to GCP.
why other options are wrong.Use Cloud CDN to cache data between the: Cloud CDN accelerates public web content delivery; it provides no internal network connectivity.

questions.questionText: Your network team has configured a Cloud Router to use an Autonomous System Number (ASN) of `65001`. Your on-premises edge router is configured with an ASN of `65002`. What type of BGP peering is established between these two routers over the VPN connection?

explanation.general explanation: When two routers communicate using BGP and they are configured with different Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs), the peering is referred to as External BGP (eBGP). Because Cloud Router (`65001`) and the on-premises router (`65002`) have different ASNs, this is an eBGP session.

why other options are wrong.iBGP (Internal BGP): iBGP is used when both routers share the exact same ASN, which is not the case here.
why other options are wrong.OSPF: OSPF is a completely different interior routing protocol, not BGP.
why other options are wrong.Static Peering: BGP is a dynamic routing protocol; static peering involves manually entering fixed IP routes without a protocol.

questions.questionText: You have configured Private Google Access for your on-premises hosts. You chose to route traffic to the `restricted.googleapis.com` virtual IP (VIP). Which Google Cloud services will your on-premises hosts be able to access using this specific VIP?
options: Only Google Cloud services that support VPC Service Controls
All Google Cloud services and consumer services like Gmail
Only Compute Engine and Cloud Storage
Only external third-party APIs published on API Gateway
correctAnswers: Only Google Cloud services that support VPC Service Controls

explanation.general explanation: The `restricted.googleapis.com` VIP is specifically designed to grant access only to Google Cloud APIs and services that support VPC Service Controls. It intentionally blocks access to consumer services (like Gmail or public YouTube) to prevent data exfiltration.

why other options are wrong.All Google Cloud services and consumer s: To access consumer services alongside GCP APIs, you would use the `private.googleapis.com` VIP instead.
why other options are wrong.Only Compute Engine and Cloud Storage: It supports many more services than just Compute and Storage, provided they support VPC Service Controls.
why other options are wrong.Only external third-party APIs published: It is used for Google-native APIs, not specifically third-party APIs.

questions.questionText: You are setting up a Partner Interconnect connection. What dynamic routing protocol must be used to exchange route information between the Google Cloud Router and your on-premises network?

explanation.general explanation: Google Cloud Router strictly utilizes the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) to exchange routing information dynamically. This applies to HA VPN, Dedicated Interconnect, and Partner Interconnect hybrid topologies.

why other options are wrong.Open Shortest Path First (OSPF): Cloud Router does not support OSPF.
why other options are wrong.Routing Information Protocol (RIP): Cloud Router does not support RIP.
why other options are wrong.Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protoc: EIGRP is a proprietary protocol (mostly Cisco) and is not supported by Google Cloud Router.
